comment: Tying a contribution to use is sound in principle but creates a free-rider problem the draft does not name. Without a duty to connect, a use-based contribution is paid by organisations that join and avoided by those that wait, so early adopters subsidise abstainers. This makes waiting individually rational and is a common reason voluntary shared infrastructure stalls at partial coverage.

public.text: Tying a contribution to use is sound in principle but creates a free-rider problem the draft does not name. Without a duty to connect, a use-based contribution is paid by organisations that join and avoided by those that wait, so early adopters subsidise abstainers. This makes waiting individually rational and is a common reason voluntary shared infrastructure stalls at partial coverage.
public.suggestedRevision: State the interaction explicitly: use-based financing requires a duty to connect to be equitable, and a duty to connect requires a right to connect to be legitimate. Recommend deciding the three together rather than sequentially. The Netherlands illustrates the failure mode - successive subsidy schemes funded participation by the willing while national coverage remained partial, because nothing obliged the remainder to join.
